newsitem.title: UK: Euro buyers make tidy profit from rising Iraqi sales.
newsitem.headline: Euro buyers make tidy profit from rising Iraqi sales.

text.p: Rising Iraqi crude oil exports are finding plenty of eager customers in Europe thanks to an aggressive pricing strategy and disruptions to Russian supply, industry sources said on Friday.

Kirkuk Blend, exported via the Turkish port of Ceyhan, traded this week at a substantial premium to Iraq's official selling price (OSP) of Dated Brent -$2.20 a barrel for May, and term contractors see little sign of the grade losing its allure.
Traders, reluctant to take the crude when sales first started at Brent less $1.55 in December, now are paying 65 cents a barrel less and keen to lay their hands on as many barrels as possible.

"Iraq is not finding it difficult at the moment because the pricing got a little bit aggressive...April was different because everybody knew May would be cheaper," said a trader at a European oil company which is a regular buyer of Iraqi crude.
Kirkuk, which tracks Saudi Arab Light prices on a cent-for-cent basis, was pegged at Dated Brent -$1.90 a barrel in April and was marked down by 30 cents for May in line with a Saudi price cut.

Oil traders say predictions that heavier Iraqi volumes would cause a downward spiral in Mediterranean sour crude prices have proved unfounded thanks to a recovery in refining margins, delays at the Black Sea port of Novorossiisk and a market contango which has encouraged companies to build stocks.

Iraq's oil minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed said on Thursday State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO) exported 750,000 barrels per day (bpd) in all last week, up from 500,000 bpd last December when the United Nations oil-for-food deal began.
Sales of Kirkuk are complemented by exports of Basrah Light from Iraq's Mina al-Bakr terminal in the Gulf.

Kirkuk volumes have risen from 300,000 bpd in March to around 400,000 bpd in April and should go even higher in May as a result of lower prices, deferred loadings and SOMO's insistence on scheduling all liftings for the first six months of the deal, which expire on June 7, by the end of May.
"If I could get my hands on some more Kirkuk I would," said a regular term lifter.
"They are sold out for May, unless there is a significant price fall, because any extra sales would mean them busting their limit."
Under the terms of the deal, Iraq is allowed to sell enough oil over six months to raise $2 billion, part of which is being used to fund food and medicine imports for the Iraqi people.

The increase in Kirkuk volumes has coincided with a recovery in regional refining margins -- cracking returns jumped to $3.70 a barrel in early April before easing to $2.70 on Thursday still $1 ahead of March's average -- and delays to loadings of Russian Urals.
Novorossiisk has been closed for about seven days already this month and the port's second biggest berth is due to shut for three weeks in May for scheduled maintenance.
"There's certainly been some extra interest in Kirkuk because people are not sure what they'll be able to get in terms of Urals," said a trader.
And with Urals talked around Dated Brent -$1.00/-$1.10, the Iraqi crude is also making much more sense in terms of refinery economics, he added.
Despite the bright picture, few term contractors expect SOMO to ask for an increase in the price for May barrels.
"Looking at it from the outside, SOMO is listening to its customers and if they are able to pocket a little money they (SOMO) have nothing against it," said one.
Traders said SOMO would be keen to smooth the way for exports in the second six-month period of the deal, which is widely expected to be renewed by the U.N.
